L120: ## TL;DR
L121: 
L122:   * We have developed a new, heuristic-based strategy for matching journal articles to their preprints. It achieved the following results on the evaluation dataset: precision 0.99, recall 0.95, F0.5 0.98. The code is available cite66†here†gitlab.com .
L123: 
L124:   * We applied the strategy to all the preprints in the Crossref database. It discovered 627K preprint–journal article relationships.
L125:   * We gathered all preprint–journal article relationships deposited by Crossref members, merged them with those discovered by the new strategy, and made everything available as cite65†a dataset†doi.org . There are 642K relationships in the dataset, including:
L126:     * 296K provided by the publisher and discovered by the strategy,
L127:     * 331K new relationships discovered by the strategy only,
L128:     * 15K provided by the publisher only.
L129:   * In the future, we plan to replace our current matching strategy with the new one and make all discovered relationships available through the Crossref REST API.
L130: ## Introduction
L131: 
L132: Relationships between preprints and journal articles link different versions of research outputs and allow one to follow the evolution of a publication over time. The Crossref deposit schema allows Crossref members to provide these relationships for new publications, either as a has-preprint relationship deposited with a journal article, or an is-preprint-of relationship deposited with a preprint.
L133: To assist members who deposit preprints, we also try to connect deposited journal articles with preprints. The current method looks for an exact match between the title and first authors. We send possible matches as suggestions to the preprint server, which decides whether to update the metadata with the relationship.
L134: At the time of writing, 137,837 journal articles in the Crossref database have a has-preprint relationship^{cite67†1 }, and 562,225 works of type posted-content (preprints belong to this type) have an is-preprint-of relationship^{cite68†2 }.
L135: We suspected that many preprint–journal article relationships are missing, as some members inevitably fail to deposit them, even after suggestions from the current matching strategy. Another factor is that the current strategy is fairly conservative, and probably misses a significant number of relationships. For these reasons, we decided to investigate whether we could improve on the current process.
L136: Doing so would allow us to infer missing relationships on a large scale, similar to how we automatically match bibliographic references to DOIs.
L137: This preprint matching task can be defined in two directions:
L138: 
L139:   * We start with a journal article and we want to find all its preprints.
L140:   * We start with a preprint and we want to find a subsequently published journal article.
L141: On the one hand, matching from journal articles to preprints would allow us to enrich the database continually with new relationships, either periodically or every time new content is added. Since journal articles tend to appear in the database later than their preprints, it makes sense for a new journal article to trigger the matching and not the other way round. This way we can expect the potential matches to be already in the database at the time of matching.
L142: On the other hand, matching from preprints to journal articles can be useful in a situation where we want to add relationships in an existing database retrospectively. In our case, the database contains many more journal articles than preprints, so for performance reasons it is better to start with preprints.
L143: 
L144: In both cases we are dealing with structured matching, meaning that we match a metadata record of a work (preprint or journal article), rather than unstructured text.

L172: We evaluated this strategy on a test set sampled from the Crossref metadata records. The test set contains 3,000 pairs (journal article, set of corresponding preprints). Half of the journal articles have known preprints and the other half don’t. The test set can be accessed cite72†here†gitlab.com .
L173: 
L174: We used precision, recall, and F0.5 as evaluation metrics:
L175:   * Precision measures the fraction of the matched relationships that are correct.
L176:   * Recall measures the fraction of the true relationships that were matched.
L177:   * F0.5 combines precision and recall in a way that favours precision.
L178: 
L179: The strategy achieved the following results: precision 0.9921, recall 0.9474, F0.5 0.9828. The average processing time was 0.96s.
L180: We have made this strategy (journal article -> preprints) available through the (experimental) API: cite73†https://marple.research.crossref.org/match?task=preprint-matching&strategy=preprint-sbmv&input=10.1109/access.2022.3213707†marple.research.crossref.org . The input is the DOI of a journal article we want to match to preprints, and the output is a list of matches found, along with the score for each.
L181: We have investigated other approaches to making decisions about which candidates to return as matches (step 3 above), including using machine learning. At present none have outperformed the heuristic approach described above. The heuristic method is also preferred because of its fast performance.
L182: ## Preprint–journal article relationship dataset
L183: 
L184: We applied the strategy to the entire Crossref database:
L185:   1. We selected all preprints published until the end of August 2023. This included only works with type posted-content and subtype preprint, as reported by the REST API. There were 1,050,247 of them.
L186:   2. We ran the matching strategy (preprint -> journal article) on them. This resulted in 627,011 preprint–journal article relationships.
L187:   3. The resulting relationships were combined with the relationships deposited by the Crossref members. We included relationships of types has-preprint or is-preprint-of, where both sides of the relationship exist in our database, were published until the end of August 2023, and are of proper types and subtypes (type=journal-article for the journal article and type=posted-content, subtype=preprint for the preprint).
L188: The resulting dataset is a single CSV file with the following fields:
L189: 
L190:   * preprint DOI (string)
L191:   * journal article DOI (string)
L192:   * whether the publisher of the journal article deposited this relationship (boolean)
L193:   * whether the publisher of the preprint deposited this relationship (boolean)
L194:   * the confidence score returned by the strategy (float, empty if the strategy did not discover this relationship)
L195: 
L196: The dataset contains:
L197:   * 641,950 relationships in total, including 580,532 preprints and 565,129 journal articles,
L198:   * 14,939 of them were deposited by the Crossref members, but not discovered by the strategy,
L199:   * 330,826 of them were discovered by the strategy, but not provided by any Crossref member,
L200:   * 296,185 of them were both deposited by a Crossref member and discovered by the strategy.
L201: 
L202: The dataset can be downloaded cite65†here†doi.org .

L119: ## Publishing preprints is about more than simply getting a DOI
L120: 
L121: Crossref can help you to clearly label content as a preprint using a preprint-specific schema. It’s not advisable to register preprints as data, components, articles, or anything else, because a preprint is not any of those things. Our service allows you to ensure the relationships between preprints and any eventual article are asserted in the metadata, and accurately readable by both humans and machines.
L122: ## Benefits of our custom support for preprints
L123:   * Persistent identifiers for preprints to ensure successful links to the scholarly record over the course of time
L124:   * The preprint-specific metadata we ask for reflects researcher workflows from preprint to formal publication
L125:   * Support for preprint versioning by providing relationships between metadata for different iterations of the same document.
L126:   * Notification of links between preprints and formal publications that may follow (such as journal articles, monographs)
L127:   * cite59†Reference linking for preprints, connecting up the scholarly record to associated literature
L128:   * cite60†Auto-update of ORCID records to ensure that preprint contributors are acknowledged for their work
L129:   * Preprints cite61†include funding data†doi.org so people can report research contributions based on funder and grant identification
L130:   * Discoverability: we make the metadata available for machine and human access, across multiple interfaces (including our cite62†REST API , cite63†OAI-PMH , and cite64†Metadata Search†search.crossref.org .
L131: ### Obligations and limitations
L132:   1. Follow the posted content cite65†metadata best practices. L133:   2. Designate a specific contact with us who will receive match notifications when an accepted manuscript (AM) or version of record (VOR) of the posted content has been registered.
L134:   3. Link your posted content record to that other record within seven days of receiving an alert.
L135:   4. Clearly label the manuscript as a preprint above the fold on its landing page, and ensure that any link to the AAM or VOR is also prominently displayed above the fold.
L136:   5. Ensure that each version is assigned a new DOI, and associate the versions via a relationship with type isVersionOf - learn more about cite66†structural metadata and cite67†declaring relationship types L137:   6. Crossmark is not currently supported for posted content.
L138:   7. You can’t add components to posted content.
L139:   8. How to register content - using the cite68†Crossref Deposit Plugin for Open Preprint Systems (OPS)†docs.pkp.sfu.ca or cite69†direct deposit of XML .
L140: ### Fees
L141: 
L142: In additional to annual membership dues, all records attract a one-time registration fee. cite70†Read about the fees. L143: 
L144: ### Key links
L145: 
L146:   * cite65†Posted content metadata best practices L147:   * How to register content via the cite68†Crossref Deposit Plugin for Open Preprint Systems (OPS)†docs.pkp.sfu.ca or cite69†direct deposit of XML L148:   * cite71†Posted content markup guide L149: ### Associating preprints with later published outputs
L150: 
L151: Once a research object has been published from the posted content and a DOI has been assigned to it, the preprint publisher will update their metadata to associate the posted content with the DOI of the accepted manuscript (AM) or version of record (VOR).
L152: We will notify the member who deposited metadata for the posted content when we find a match between the title and first author of two publications, so that the potential relationship can be reviewed. The posted content publisher must then update the preprint metadata record by declaring the AM/VOR relationship. The notification is delivered by email to the technical contact on file. Please cite6†contact us if you need the email notifications to be sent to a different address.
